## Introduction

<!----
- Possible prompts:
  - Review a text, maybe a Markdown, maybe a Word doc
----->

### Learning goals

In this lecture, you will learn how to:

- Set up and use the Claude Code extension in VS Code Server at OSC
- Use Claude to ask questions about, write, and edit code, with your files as context
- Let Claude act as an "agent" that runs commands,
  and control what it may do with permission modes
- Give Claude persistent instructions (ones that carry over between conversations) with a `CLAUDE.md` file
- Manage Claude's context window and costs

### From chat to agents

In [the previous lecture](./w8a_genAI.qmd), you used genAI through a browser-based chat.
That works well for many questions, but when coding, it has clear limitations:
the model can't see your files unless you paste or upload them,
and it can't check whether the code it writes actually works.

Today, we'll use **Claude Code**, Anthropic's "agentic" coding tool.
Working inside your editor, it can:

- **Read** the files in your project, so you don't have to explain or paste them
- **Edit and create** files, showing you each change for approval
- **Run commands** in the terminal, for example to test a script or check a program's
  help info

In other words, if browser chat is like emailing a knowledgeable colleague,
working with an agent is more like having them sit next to you at your computer.

### Why Claude Code in VS Code?

There are many AI coding tools, but this setup has two key advantages for us:

- **It's approved for your research data.**\
  Rather than using a personal account, we'll authenticate through an API key from OSU's
  [Generative AI Service {{< fa external-link >}}](https://it.osu.edu/generative-ai-service),
  which is approved for use with restricted institutional data.

- **Integration within our current VS Code setup.**\
  We'll only have to install one extension.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note}
#### Inline suggestions, GitHub Copilot, and other Claude Code programs

Another kind of AI coding help in IDEs is **inline suggestions**:
"ghost text" that appears as you type and that you can accept with <kbd>Tab</kbd>.
Claude Code does not offer these, but some other tools do, for example GitHub Copilot.
**GitHub Copilot** is built into VS Code, including VS Code Server at OSC.
If you want to try inline suggestions, see the
[self-study page on GitHub Copilot](/bonus/copilot.qmd).

Claude Code itself also comes in several forms,
including a command-line program and a desktop app.
Here, we'll use its VS Code extension.
:::

## Getting set up

### Prepare and open a dir for this week

1. At <https://ondemand.osc.edu>, start a VS Code session in `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER`.

2. In the terminal, create a dir for this week, and copy your FastQC script from last week into it:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p week08/scripts
   cp -v week07/scripts/fastqc.sh week08/scripts/
   ```
   ```bash-out
   'week07/scripts/fastqc.sh' -> 'week08/scripts/fastqc.sh'
   ```

3. Open the `week08` dir as your VS Code folder with `File` > `Open Folder`.

   ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
   Claude treats the folder that is open in VS Code as its "**workspace**":
   this is where it will look for files,
   and by default the only place where it can make changes.
   (Yet another application where good project organization,
   in the sense of having a single self-contained dir with all project files,
   pays off.)
   :::

### Connect Claude to your API key

You've received a **personal API key** from us,
giving you access to Claude models through OSU's Generative AI Service.

To tell Claude to use your key,
you need to create a **settings file** in your Home dir.
Claude expects this file to be a JSON file at the standard location
`~/.claude/settings.json`, and will read that file every time it starts up.
Let's set this up:

1. Copy a template settings file to that location:

   ```bash
   mkdir -p ~/.claude
   cp /fs/ess/PAS3493/share/claude-settings.json ~/.claude/settings.json
   ```

2. Open your copy of the settings file in the editor^[
     as before, use <kbd>Ctrl/Cmd</kbd> + click in the terminal,
     or click `File` > `Open File` > type `~/.claude/settings.json`.].

3. In the file, **replace the placeholder** `<API-KEY>` with your personal API key
   in the manner shown below:

   ```{.file filename="&#126;/.claude/settings.json (excerpt - before)"}
     "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "<API-KEY>",
   ```

   ```{.file filename="&#126;/.claude/settings.json (excerpt - after - with fictional API key)"}
     "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "bY-7jiuWbfck9DZk34hA_t",
   ```


::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More about the settings file _(Click to expand)_

Here is what the file looks like before you add your own key:

```{.json .file filename="&#126;/.claude/settings.json"}
{
  "env": {
    "ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL": "https://litellm.cloud.osu.edu",
    "ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN": "<API-KEY>",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL": "claude-opus-5-5",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_SONNET_MODEL": "claude-sonnet-5",
    "ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_HAIKU_MODEL": "claude-haiku-5-5",
    "CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS": "1"
  },
  "model": "sonnet",
  "effortLevel": "medium",
  "outputStyle": "Concise",
  "theme": "auto"
}
```

<!---
Note for self: sonnet-5-5 and sonnet-5.5 are listed as possible models,
but don't seem to work.
---->

The file is in JSON format, a plain-text format with key-value pairs:
a colon `:` separates each key from its value, pairs are separated by commas,
and curly braces `{}` group pairs.
A single missing quote or comma breaks the whole file
(this would be a likely culprit if Claude doesn't pick up your API key).

- `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` makes Claude go through OSU's service rather than
  directly to Anthropic.
- `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` is the API key.
- The `MODEL` lines specify which model versions to use.

:::

::: callout-important
#### Treat the API key like a password
Anyone with your key can use it, and usage costs money and depletes your key's budget.
So never share your key or commit it to a Git repository.
That's one reason the settings file is located in your Home dir,
and not in a project dir that others can see.
:::

### The prompt box

Most of what you'll do with Claude starts from the prompt box:

![](/img/claude-prompt-box2.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the Claude Code prompt box." .lightbox}

You can type a prompt (question) in the box,
and press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to send it to Claude,
or click the upward arrow in the bottom-right corner of the box.
We'll go over the other buttons across the bottom of the box in more detail below
--- but briefly, from left to right:

- **`+`** adds **files** as context to your prompt.
- **`/`** opens the so-called *command menu*,
  which is really a collection of nearly all options and settings in Claude Code,
  including those that can be accessed with the other buttons.
  You'll need this one least often.
- Once Claude has responded, a **clock icon** with a number of minutes appears.
  This shows how long until the conversation's "cache" expires,
  after which your next message will be more expensive
  (see the box on caching in [Managing context and cost](#managing-context-and-cost)).
- `Sonnet 5 Medium` is the current **model** and **effort level**,
  and you can click on it to change them.
- **`Manual`** is the current **permission mode** (what Claude is allowed to do),
  and you can click on it to change it.

### A quick test

To check that Claude works, type this prompt and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>:

> Write a limerick about a grad student whose shell script keeps failing

If you get a limerick back, Claude is set up correctly.
If you get an error instead, or it **merely keeps printing verbs** like "Brewing"
and "Deliberating" (Claude's variant on a spinning wheel) but nothing else,
let us know, and we'll help you troubleshoot.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

![](/img/claude-limerick-prompt.png){fig-align="center" width="98%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a prompt to Claude asking for a limerick about a grad student whose shell script keeps failing, and the response from Claude." .lightbox}

::: legend2
Write or paste the prompt in the box, and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>.
:::

:::
::: {.column}

![](/img/claude-limerick-reply.png){fig-align="center" width="98%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a limerick about a grad student whose shell script keeps failing, written by Claude." .lightbox}

::: legend2
Then, your question and, after a while, the answer should appear in the panel
above the prompt box.
:::

:::
:::

### Managing conversations

You can manage your conversations using buttons at the top of the panel,
as shown in this screenshot:

![](/img/claude-top-icons.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the buttons at the top of the Claude panel." .lightbox}

::: legend2
In the bottom-right, the bookmark, clock/history,
and new conversation buttons are shown.
:::


From left to right:

- The **bookmark** icon lets you access specific answers from Claude that you
  previously bookmarked
  (using a similar icon that appears below an answer when you hover over it).
- The **clock icon** lists your previous conversations, in case you want to return to one^[
    Conversations are given a default name based on the first prompt you sent,
    as also visible in the screenshot above,
    but these names can be changed by clicking the pencil icon next to them.].
- The **chat icon** with a `+` starts a new conversation.
  Start a new one for **each new task** (you'll see why [later](#start-fresh)).

::: {.callout-tip}
#### The exact interface is ever-changing
For example, the bookmarking feature was added in a recent update.
These screenshots were made just days before class,
and are likely to reflect what we'll see in class,
but you may well see differences in a later version of the extension.
:::

### More on models and effort levels

Click on `Sonnet 5 Medium` in the bottom-right of the prompt box
to open the model and effort menu:

![](/img/claude-model-selection.png){fig-align="center" width="65%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the Claude Code model selection menu, with entries for Default, Opus 5.5, Fable, Sonnet 5 (checked), and Haiku 5.5, followed by an Effort slider and an Ultracode toggle." .lightbox}

**Models** ---
The checkmark shows the model you're currently using.
Claude comes in four model "sizes", listed here from most to least capable:

- *Fable*: the most capable and by far the most expensive model.
  Meant for very hard and long-running tasks,
  so you're unlikely to need it in this course (I've never used it).
- *Opus*: very capable, but slower and more expensive than Sonnet.
  Can be worth it for more complex questions.
- *Sonnet*: fast, capable, and much cheaper.
  Plenty for writing and editing scripts like ours.
  This is the **default** we've set in the settings file,
  and the one you should use most of the time.
- *Haiku*: the fastest and cheapest, for simple questions and quick edits.

::: callout-warning
#### Two things in this menu can be confusing:

- The **"Default (recommended)"** entry at the top is _not_ the model you set
  in your settings file.
  It is Claude Code's own built-in default (currently Opus),
  which it would use if you hadn't picked a model at all.
  Selecting it switches you to Opus, so you'll use up your budget faster ---
  not recommended except when you think you really need a more capable model.
- Most entries say **"Custom ... model"**.
  This is because our settings file specifies exactly which model version
  each size should use (the `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_..._MODEL` lines).

:::

**Effort** ---
How much the model "thinks" before responding:
Low, Medium, High, Extra-high, or Max.
More effort can give better answers to hard problems,
but is slower and uses more tokens. Medium is a good default for our purposes.

**Ultracode** ---
A brand-new toggle that is separate from the effort level.
When it's on, Claude handles every substantial task with a so-called
"workflow": a script that runs many Claude "subagents" in parallel,
for example one per file, plus agents that double-check each other's work.
This is meant for large jobs such as auditing or modifying hundreds of files,
and it makes each request use many more tokens and take longer.
**Keep it off.**

_In summary, we'll stick to our settings file's default of Sonnet 5 Medium for now,_
_but now you know how to change it if you want to try a different model or effort level._

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### What about a "Thinking" toggle? _(Click to expand)_

Earlier versions of Claude Code had a separate toggle to turn "thinking"
on or off, and you may still see it in online tutorials and videos.
This toggle has disappeared because recent Claude models always think,
and decide for themselves how much thinking each step needs.
The effort level is now _the_ way to control this:
a lower effort level means less thinking,
and a higher one means more.
:::

## A first prompt: writing a script

### Ask Claude to write a script

Start a new conversation with the `+` icon, and submit the following prompt:

> Write a script scripts/count_reads.sh that counts the number of reads in a
> gzipped FASTQ file. The FASTQ file should be an argument to the script.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

Claude will show you what it's doing as it goes,
and it will likely **ask you for permission** to run a command,
like in the screenshot on the right,
where it started by wanting to check if the `scripts` dir that we asked to put
the script in already exists, and create it if not.

Try to understand what it is proposing to do, and click **Yes** to let it run the command.

In general, Claude loves to use **shell commands** for many tasks,
so, as it happens, you have a leg up on better understanding what it does given
what you've learned in this course.

:::
::: {.column width="55%"}

![](/img/claude-ask-permission1.png){fig-align="center" width="95%" fig-alt="A screenshot of a Claude Code permission request to run a command." .lightbox}

:::
:::

It should then **ask for permission** to create the script file,
and show the proposed contents in the "diff" format we've seen before:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}

![](/img/claude-allow-write.png){fig-align="center" width="95%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a Claude Code permission request to write a file." .lightbox}

:::
::: {.column width="58%"}

![](/img/claude-new-script.png){fig-align="center" width="100%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a Claude Code permission request to write a file, showing the proposed contents of the new script." .lightbox}

:::
:::

You can accept the change, decline it,
or decline it and tell Claude what to do differently.
Take a quick look and accept it ---
you'll take a closer look in the upcoming exercise.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}

Claude may also ask to make the script **executable** with `chmod +x`,
and if so, you can allow it to do that as well.

_(Making scripts executable is not really necessary,_
_so we didn't practice with this in class._
_But it can be a convenience in some contexts ---_
_see [this box](/week07/w7a_scripts1.qmd#run-without-bash) from last week for more.)_

:::
::: {.column width="60%"}

![](/img/claude-make-executable.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="A screenshot of a Claude Code permission request to run a command to make the new script executable." .lightbox}

:::
:::

When Claude is done, it may close the script in the editor pane,
but it should provide a clickable link in the panel:

![](/img/claude-clickable-file-link.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a clickable link to the new script in the Claude Code panel." .lightbox}

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 1: Trying out Claude Code (breakout rooms)

1. Discuss the script Claude wrote:
   - Does the script look reasonable? Do you understand every line?
     It's likely you don't, because the script probably uses a few constructs
     that were only discussed in optional reading material
     ([command substitution](/bonus/shell-scripting.html#command-substitution)
     and [bash arithmetic](/bonus/shell-scripting.html#arithmetic)).
     You can ask Claude to explain any line you don't understand.

   - Did you all get the same script? If not, can you make sense of the differences?

   - Did Claude look at other files in your workspace before writing the script?
     If so, does that seem to have affected the way it wrote the script?
     If not, how does the script compare the `fastqc.sh` script we wrote in week 7,
     for example in terms of structure, header lines, and so on?

   - How does it compare to the script Gemini wrote for the same task in the previous lecture?

   - Did Claude test the script, or offer to, for any of you?

   <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} Click here for a hint</summary>

   When I ran this, Claude reported finding the `fastqc.sh` script in the `scripts`
   dir, and said it would copy the style of that script:

   ![](/img/claude-copying-script-style.png){fig-align="center" width="70%" fig-alt="A screenshot of Claude Code reporting that it is copying the style of an existing script." .lightbox}

   The resulting script from the earlier screenshot indeed very closely resembles
   the `fastqc.sh` script in its structure.

   </details>

2. Run the script on one of the FASTQ files, like `../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz`.
   Did it work and can you check whether the number it reports is correct?

   <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} Click here for some hints</summary>

   Here is how you can run the script for that file:

   ```bash
   bash scripts/count_reads.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
   ```

   The correct number of reads is 500,000,
   and this can be checked with `zcat` and `wc -l`:

   ```bash
   zcat ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz | wc -l
   ```
   ```bash-out
   2000000
   ```

   The number of reads is the number of lines (2,000,000) divided by 4.

   </details>

3. Probably, Claude followed the style of the `fastqc.sh` script for most of you,
   but its logging output is a bit verbose for a simple "utility" script like this.
   Either way, let's say we're picky about the output format of the script,
   but failed to mention that in our initial prompt to Claude.
   Ask Claude to change the script:

   > Change the output so it only prints the file name and the number of reads, separated by a space

   ::: {.columns}
   ::: {.column width="42%"}

   As you'd expect, Claude will realize you're talking about the script it just wrote,
   but if you have the script open,
   Claude will also automatically add it as explicit "context" to your prompt:
   its filename is shown below the prompt box (more on this below).

   :::
   ::: {.column width="58%"}

   ![](/img/claude-context-init.png){fig-align="center" width="95%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the Claude Code prompt box showing that the script file is added as context." .lightbox}

   ::: legend2
   `count_reads.sh` is automatically added as context to your prompt when you
   have the file open.
   The clock icon (`4m`) shows the time left before the cache expires
   (see [Managing context and cost](#managing-context-and-cost)).
   :::

   :::
   :::

4. Do you understand how Claude shows the proposed changes to the script?
   And do you understand the actual changes it made to the script?

   <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} Click here for some hints</summary>

   ::: {.columns}
   ::: {.column width="38%"}

   The screenshot on the right is the "diff" it showed for me,
   with proposed deletions (all the logging lines) highlighted in **red**,
   and additions (a single replacement line) highlighted in **green**.

   Those changes are in two separate places in the script,
   and each of them _can_ be separately accepted or rejected by clicking the
   checkmark (✓) or backward arrow (↶) in the added gray boxes below them.

   (On the other hand, if you click "Yes" in the Claude Code prompt box,
   it will accept all changes at once. That's a more typical way of working,
   though it's useful to know that you can accept or reject individual changes.)

   :::
   ::: {.column width="58%"}

   ![](/img/claude-diff-narrow.png){fig-align="center" width="95%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the proposed changes to the script, showing a diff." .lightbox}

   :::
   :::

   </details>

5. Ask Claude to make one more change:

   > Make the script accept multiple FASTQ files, and print one line per file

   Look at how Claude made the script accept multiple files,
   and try to understand this mechanism ---
   you can ask Claude (or Gemini) to explain it.
   And does it use a `for` loop like we did in week 7?

6. With a single command, run the script on all garrigos R1 files at once.
   You should know how to do this, but you can also ask Claude for help if you want.

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} Click here for the solution</summary>

   ```bash
   bash scripts/count_reads.sh ../garrigos/fastq/*_R1.fastq.gz
   ```

   </details>

7. Reflect on the difference between running the same task on many files with a
   `for` loop **inside** the script (like here) versus **outside** the script
   (like we did in week 7).

   <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} Click here for some hints</summary>

   It should be clear that once the script is written,
   it is more convenient to have the loop inside the script.

   However, we talked about, though haven't yet practiced with,
   submitting jobs to a cluster with `sbatch`.
   What is a key difference then?

   Given that, when does it make sense to have the loop inside the script,
   and when does it make sense to have it outside?

   </details>

:::

::: {.callout-tip}
#### These prompts were deliberately simple
They let us focus on understanding how the tool works,
and see what it can do and explore when we're not very specific about what we want.
But if you know what you want, or have information that might help Claude help you
figure that out, it's often worth giving more context and detail,
as discussed in [the previous lecture](./w8a_genAI.qmd).
:::

## Your files as context

### Your workspace is the context

A key advantage of using AI inside your editor is that your files are readily available:
you don't need to upload or copy-and-paste them.
Your entire **workspace** (the folder open in VS Code) is "implicit" context:
when Claude thinks it's useful, it will search and read files there by itself.

However, when you have a specific task and specific files in mind,
it's often better to point Claude to the relevant files **explicitly**.
That's faster and cheaper,
and avoids Claude making assumptions about which files you mean.

### Adding files and code to your prompt

- **The file that's active in the editor** is added automatically.
  You can see this below the prompt box
  (to remove the file as context, click the `x` next to it).

  ![](/img/claude-automatic-file-context2.png){fig-align="center" width="65%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the Claude Code prompt box showing that the file open in the editor was added as context." .lightbox}

- **Selected lines** in the editor are also added automatically.
  This is handy to ask about specific lines in a longer script:

  ![](/img/claude-select-lines2.png){fig-align="center" width="65%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the Claude Code prompt box showing that a selection of lines was added as context." .lightbox}

- **Type `@`** followed by part of a file name to add any file in your workspace,
  including files in subdirs.
  You can also wait for the list to appear after typing `@`,
  as shown in the screenshot below.

  ![](/img/claude-context-add3.png){fig-align="center" width="45%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the file list that appears after typing @ in the Claude Code prompt box." .lightbox}

- When you switch to a different file in the editor,
  Claude will _swap_ the context to that file,
  and it won't keep the previous file in context.
  To add **multiple files**, either type `@` as well,
  or press <kbd>Alt/Option</kbd>+<kbd>K</kbd> while in a file:
  this keeps it in the context, even when you switch to another file.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### The `+` button _(Click to expand)_

You can also add context with the `+` button below the prompt box.
This also lets you upload files from your own computer.

![](/img/claude-context-add1.png){fig-align="center" width="30%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the menu that appears after clicking the plus button in the Claude Code prompt box." .lightbox}
:::

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 2: Ask about your code

1. Start a new conversation.
   Then, open your `scripts/fastqc.sh` (copied from week 7) in the editor, and ask Claude:

   > Explain what this script does, line by line

   Does its explanation match your own understanding?

2. Select the first line with `apptainer exec` (the one that runs FastQC) in the editor, and ask:

   > What does this line do, and why do we need apptainer here?

3. The command below "accidentally" omits the output dir argument
   that needs to be passed to the script along with the FASTQ file.
   Before you run it, predict what will happen. Then run it:

   ```bash
   bash scripts/fastqc.sh ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz
   ```

   Copy the error message into the prompt box (with the script still open;
   you can add a question like "What went wrong", but this doesn't tend to be necessary).
   Does its explanation match your prediction?

4. Close all files in the editor, and ask:

   > Which scripts in this project use a container, and for which program versions?

   Watch how Claude finds the answer.

5. First, predict: would your `fastqc.sh` still work if a FASTQ file name contained a space?
   Then ask Claude:

   > Which scripts in this project would break if a FASTQ file name contained a space?

   Which files does Claude look at?
   Does its answer match your prediction?

<!----
<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} Click here for the solution</summary>

3. The error is `$2: unbound variable`: the script assigns `outdir="$2"`,
   but no second argument was given, and because of `set -u`, Bash stops with an error
   when it encounters an unset variable.
   Claude may offer to add a "usage" check that prints a helpful message when arguments
   are missing. That's a reasonable improvement, but it's your call whether to accept it.

4. Claude will search the `scripts` dir (e.g., for `apptainer` or `oras://`),
   read the matching scripts, and report the container URLs, which include the program versions.

5. `fastqc.sh` quotes its variables (`"$fastq"`, `"$outdir"`), so it handles spaces fine.
   Whether `count_reads.sh` does depends on the script Claude wrote.
   If Claude reports a problem in `fastqc.sh` anyway,
   that's a good reminder that you should check its claims.

</details>
---->
:::

## Permission modes and running commands

### Permission modes {#permission-modes}

The permission mode, shown at the bottom right of the prompt box,
determines what Claude may do **without asking you first**.
Click on it to switch between modes:

- **Manual**: Claude asks permission for each file edit and for many commands
  (it runs simple read-only commands, like `ls`, `head`, and `grep`, without asking,
  as you should have noticed in the previous exercises).

- **Edit automatically**: Claude edits files and runs simple file commands
  like `mkdir` and `cp` in your workspace without asking.

- **Auto**: Claude decides for itself when to ask for permission.

- **Plan**: Claude doesn't change anything, but writes a plan,
  which opens as a Markdown document that you can review and modify before
  Claude carries it out.
  This is useful for bigger tasks and is covered in more detail in
  [the self-study page on Claude Code](../bonus/claude-code.qmd#plan-mode).

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-tip}
#### For now, we'll stick to Manual mode

It's slower-going, but you'll see exactly what Claude does.
Once you're comfortable reviewing Claude's work, though,
the many permission requests can become tedious,
and it's easy to start clicking "Yes" without really reading what you approve.

At that point, "**Auto mode**" is a good alternative.
In this mode, a separate AI model checks each action before it runs:
routine actions, like editing files in your project, are permitted without asking,
while risky ones, like deleting many files or doing things you didn't ask for, are blocked.
:::

### Letting Claude run commands

We've already seen how Claude runs commands,
for example to check whether a directory or certain files exist.
As you might expect then,
we can also ask Claude directly to run commands on our behalf --- try this:

> Run count_reads.sh on all FASTQ files in ../garrigos/fastq, and tell me which sample has the fewest reads

Before running the script, Claude will show you the exact command and ask for permission.
Because the FASTQ files are outside your workspace,
it may also ask for permission to access that dir.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}

You'll typically see these options:

- **"Yes"**: run the command this once.
- **"Yes, allow ... for this project (just you)"**:
  also allow this command in the future, without asking.
- **No**: don't run it. You can add a note to tell Claude what to do instead.

(Claude may also ask for permission to search the **web** or fetch a web page,
for example to look up a program's documentation.)

:::
::: {.column width="58%"}

![](/img/claude-asks.png){fig-align="center" width="95%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of a Claude Code permission request to run a command." .lightbox}

:::
:::

Here, click one of the two affirmative options to let Claude run the command.
Is the output correct?
Here's what I got --- it's indeed correct, and it even correctly inferred that
these reads were "subsampled to a fixed depth":

![](/img/claude-run-command-result.png){fig-align="center" width="65%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of the result of a command run by Claude." .lightbox}

::: callout-warning
#### Cautionary notes

**Letting Claude produce results vs. code**\
In the example above, we've let Claude report a _result_ directly,
to see how it runs commands.
For your research, this is **not** good practice,
or at least it isn't for producing final results you intend to report.
Instead, your routine should be to have Claude write the _code_ that produces
your results, so that you can check, rerun, and keep it.

**Read every command before you approve it**\
Be especially careful with commands that delete, move, or overwrite files,
that change things outside your workspace, that push to GitHub,
or submit many jobs at once.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Use Git as a safety net _(Click to expand)_
Version control pairs very well with agentic AI:
commit your work before asking Claude for a bigger change,
review all of its changes afterwards with `git diff` or the Source Control panel,
and undo anything you don't want with `git restore <file>`.
For more on this and other guardrails, such as permission rules that block specific actions,
see the [self-study page on Claude Code](../bonus/claude-code.qmd#guardrails).
:::

### Getting answers from a program's help info {#help-info}

In the previous lecture, we talked about hallucinations,
like a chatbot making up program options that don't actually exist.
An example was the question about TrimGalore and two-color chemistry,
for which Microsoft Copilot made up a `--polyG` option last year.

A chatbot can only answer such questions based on its training data
(or perhaps a web search),
but an agent that can run commands can instead look up the program's **actual help info**,
and be sure to look at the right version of the program.
Start a new conversation, and ask the TrimGalore question again ---
this time pointing Claude to a container with the program:

> How can I tell TrimGalore that my reads use Illumina two-color chemistry?
> Check the help info using this container:
> oras://community.wave.seqera.io/library/trim-galore:2.3.0--a56e49e832976df4

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise 1: Let Claude fix a broken script

1. Create a new file `scripts/read_summary.sh` and paste the following into it.
   This script should count the number of reads in every FASTQ file in a dir,
   but it contains (at least) one error:

   ```{.bash .file filename="scripts/read_summary.sh"}
   #!/bin/bash
   set -euo pipefail

   # Copy the placeholder variables
   fastq_dir="$1"
   outfile="$2"

   # Initial logging
   echo "Starting script read_summary.sh"
   date
   echo "Input FASTQ dir:    $fastq_dir"
   echo "Output file:        $outfile"
   echo

   # Count the number of reads in each FASTQ file
   for fastq in "$fastq_dir/*.fastq.gz"; do
       n_lines=$(cat "$fastq" | wc -l)
       n_reads=$(( n_lines / 4 ))
       echo -e "$(basename "$fastq")\t$n_reads" >> "$outfile"
   done

   # Final logging
   echo "Successfully finished script read_summary.sh"
   date
   ```

2. Run the script, and take a look at the error:

   ```bash
   bash scripts/read_summary.sh ../garrigos/fastq read_summary.tsv
   ```

3. Start a new conversation, open the script in the editor, and ask Claude to fix it
   by pasting the error message along with a short prompt like:

   > I got this error when running this script with
   > `bash scripts/read_summary.sh ../garrigos/fastq read_summary.tsv`. Please fix it.
   > [paste the error message here]

   Then watch what Claude does:

   - Does it explain the cause of the error, and do you understand the explanation?
   - Does it only fix the error you reported, or does it find and fix other problems too?
   - Does it run the script to test its fix?

4. If Claude did not test the script, run it yourself.
   Then check the contents of `read_summary.tsv`: are the read counts correct?
   If the counts are not correct, tell Claude, and let it fix the script.

<!----
<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} Click here for the solution</summary>

The script contains two errors:

- The glob in the `for` loop is inside double quotes (`"$fastq_dir/*.fastq.gz"`),
  so it is not expanded.
  The loop therefore runs only once, with the literal string `../garrigos/fastq/*.fastq.gz`,
  and `cat` fails because no file has that name.
  The fix is to keep the `*` outside the quotes: `"$fastq_dir"/*.fastq.gz`.

- The script uses `cat` instead of `zcat` on gzipped files.
  This doesn't cause an error message:
  `wc -l` simply counts the "lines" in the compressed data,
  so the script reports read counts that are far too low.
  This is the more dangerous of the two errors, because it silently produces wrong results.

Claude may have spotted the second error just by reading the script,
or only after running it and seeing suspicious read counts --- or not at all,
if it didn't test the script.
This shows why a script that runs without errors still needs to be checked,
whether you or Claude wrote or fixed it.

Finally, because the script appends (`>>`) to the output file,
running it multiple times will add the same files again to `read_summary.tsv`.
Claude may have noticed this when testing the script,
and either removed the file between test runs or changed `>>` to something else.

</details>
---->
:::

### Stopping, steering, and rewinding

Sometimes you notice that Claude misunderstood you, or is going down the wrong path
(it's often worth keeping a close eye on its "thinking" as it works!).
In those cases, you don't have to wait for it to finish:

- **Steer it**: type a new message while Claude is working,
  and it will take that into account before continuing.

  ![The message "actually load R 4.4.0 instead" was added while Claude was working.](/img/claude-interrupt1.png){fig-align="center" width="65%" fig-alt="A screenshot of a message being sent to Claude while it is working." .lightbox}

- **Stop it**: press <kbd>Esc</kbd> (or click the stop button).
  You can then send a new message to redirect it.

- **Rewind**: press <kbd>Esc</kbd> twice in quick succession,
  or hover over one of your earlier messages and click the rewind button,
  to go back to an earlier point in the conversation.
  You can choose to also *undo the file changes* Claude made after that point ---
  but only changes made with Claude's own file edits:
  changes made by *commands* it ran are not undone.

  ![](/img/claude-interrupt2.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the Claude Code rewind menu, listing earlier messages to go back to." .lightbox}

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise 2: Rewind

1. Start a new conversation, and ask Claude:

   > Add a comment above every line of scripts/count_reads.sh explaining what it does.
   > Then run the script on ../garrigos/fastq/S63_R1.fastq.gz,
   > redirecting its output to read_counts.txt.

   Accept the edit and the command, and check that both changes were made.

2. Before you rewind, predict which of the two changes will be undone.

3. Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> <kbd>Esc</kbd>, rewind to before this prompt,
   and check both files. Was your prediction correct?

<!----
<details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} Click here for the solution</summary>

3. The comments in `count_reads.sh` are gone, because Claude added them with its own file edit.
   But `read_counts.txt` still exists, because it was created by a command
   (with the `>` redirection), and rewinding doesn't undo the effects of commands.

</details>
---->
:::

## Persistent instructions with `CLAUDE.md`

### Why persistent instructions?

Each new conversation with Claude starts with an empty context window:
it doesn't see what you discussed in earlier conversations.
So you may find yourself repeatedly telling it the same things, such as:

- "Run programs with Apptainer containers, not by installing them"
- "Never modify the raw data in `../garrigos`"
- "Follow such and such script conventions"

Rather than repeating yourself,
you can put these kinds of instructions in a file called `CLAUDE.md`
to make them "persistent" across conversations.

### What is `CLAUDE.md`?

`CLAUDE.md` is a Markdown file that Claude
**automatically reads** at the start of every conversation in your project.
There is no required format, but it should be concise and easy to read,
for you as well as for Claude^[
  Many other AI coding tools use a similar file called `AGENTS.md`.
  Claude reads that file too, but by default only if there is no `CLAUDE.md`.].
Typically, it's placed in **a project's root dir**, like our `week08` dir:

```bash-out-solo
week08
├── CLAUDE.md
└── scripts
    ├── count_reads.sh
    ├── fastqc.sh
    └── read_summary.sh
```

### What to include in `CLAUDE.md`

Some useful things to include in a `CLAUDE.md` are:

- **Project overview**: the research question, organism, data type, and experimental design.
- **Key dirs and files**: where the raw data, scripts, and results are.
- **Conventions**: how you write scripts and name files.
- **Software**: how software is run (e.g., with containers) and which versions.
- **Rules and pitfalls**: things Claude should never do, or tends to get wrong.

### Creating a `CLAUDE.md` with `/init`

You can write a `CLAUDE.md` by hand, but it can be easier to get started with
the **`/init`** command:
Claude looks through your project and drafts a `CLAUDE.md` for you to review and edit^[
  If a `CLAUDE.md` already exists, `/init` will instead suggest updates to it.].

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 3: Create and use a `CLAUDE.md`

1. Type `/init` in the prompt box and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>.
   Once Claude is done, open the `CLAUDE.md` file it created.

   - Is what it wrote correct?
   - How much of it is information that Claude could also have gotten by simply
     reading the files in your project?
   - What important information about your project is missing,
     because it can't be found in these files?

   In a small practice project like ours, `/init` doesn't have much to work with,
   so its draft will mostly describe the existing scripts.
   It's more useful in larger projects, but even there,
   the most valuable parts of a `CLAUDE.md` are things only you know:
   what the project is about, where the data is, and how you want things done.

2. To see that Claude really reads this file, add the following lines at the end of
   `CLAUDE.md`, and save the file:

   ```{.markdown .file filename="CLAUDE.md"}
   ### Replies

   - Always answer in the style of a pirate
   ```

   Then, start a new conversation, and ask:

   > What does `set -u` do in a shell script?

   Followed by:

   > Why are you talking like that?

   Afterwards, remove the pirate lines from `CLAUDE.md`.

   <details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} Click to see what it told me</summary>

   ![](/img/claude-pirate.png){fig-align="center" width="65%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of Claude Code answering a question in pirate style." .lightbox}

   ![](/img/claude-pirate2.png){fig-align="center" width="65%" .no-border fig-alt="A screenshot of Claude Code answering a follow-up question in pirate style." .lightbox}

   </details>

3. Replace the entire contents of `CLAUDE.md` with the following,
   which adds information that `/init` couldn't know about:

   ```{.markdown .file filename="CLAUDE.md"}
   # Practice RNA-Seq project

   Practice project for the course PLNTPTH 5006, using RNA-Seq data from
   Garrigós et al. (2025) on *Culex pipiens* mosquitoes
   infected with two avian *Plasmodium* species.

   ## Data

   - The FASTQ files are in `../garrigos/fastq`:
     paired-end, ~75-bp Illumina reads for 22 samples,
     subsampled to 500,000 reads per file, with names like `S63_R1.fastq.gz`
   - Sample metadata is in `../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv`
   - Never modify, move, or delete anything in `../garrigos`

   ## Dirs

   - `scripts/`: shell scripts
   - `results/`: all output, in a separate subdir for each step (e.g. `results/fastqc`)

   ## Software

   - We work at the Ohio Supercomputer Center (OSC)
   - Run programs with Apptainer containers from Seqera Containers (`oras://` URLs),
     not with `module load` or by installing them
   - Don't use multi-threading options unless asked

   ## Shell script conventions

   - Start scripts with `#!/bin/bash` and `set -euo pipefail`
   - Below that, add a comment block with the script's purpose and an example command to run it
   - Copy arguments to descriptively named, lowercase variables (e.g. `fastq="$1"`);
     use uppercase only for constants (e.g. `CONTAINER=...`)
   - At the start, report the script name, the date, and the inputs;
     at the end, report the program version, a success message, and the date
   - Create output dirs with `mkdir -p` before writing to them
   ```

4. Start another new conversation, so that Claude reads the updated `CLAUDE.md`, and ask:

   > Write a script that takes the first 10,000 reads of a FASTQ file,
   > and run it on the R1 file of sample S63

   Notice that this prompt doesn't say where the FASTQ files are,
   where the output should go, or how to write the script.

5. Check the result:
   - Did Claude know where to find the FASTQ file, or did it have to search for it?
     And where did it put the output?
   - Check the script against each of the conventions. Which did Claude follow?
     Do all of them make sense for this particular script ---
     and if not, how did Claude handle that?
   - Is the output correct? Check that the output file has 40,000 lines
     (use `zcat` if it is compressed).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More on using `CLAUDE.md` _(Click to expand)_

**Keep updating your `CLAUDE.md`**\
Start simple, and add to it whenever you notice yourself telling Claude the
same thing again, or Claude making the same mistake again.
Be mindful of its length, though:
it's read at the start of every conversation, so it uses up tokens each time.

-----

**Other locations for `CLAUDE.md` files**\
You can also put a `CLAUDE.md` in a parent dir, to apply to several related projects,
or at `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, to apply to all your projects.
See the [documentation on `CLAUDE.md`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory) for details.

------

**Instructions are not strict rules**\
`CLAUDE.md` contains _instructions_, which Claude will usually but not always follow.
To strictly enforce rules, use [permission rules](../bonus/claude-code.qmd#permission-rules).
For instructions that you only need for _specific_ tasks,
see the self-study page on [skills](../bonus/claude-code.qmd#skills).

-----

**`CLAUDE.md` vs. Claude's memory**\
Besides reading your `CLAUDE.md`, Claude also keeps **memory** notes for itself:
when you correct it or tell it about your preferences, it _may_ save a note,
which is loaded into future conversations in the same project.
You can also ask it directly to save memories, e.g. _"Remember that I prefer ..."_.
Like `CLAUDE.md`, memory notes are plain Markdown files,
and they're stored in your Home dir.
Claude writes them itself, but it's worth checking them now and then.

More broadly, memory notes are another big advantage of AI in your editor.
While browser-based chatbots may remember general things about you,
here you can save more extensive, specific information about your project and your preferences.
You can check Claude's memory notes by typing `/memory` in the prompt box.
More details are on the [self-study page](../bonus/claude-code.qmd#memory).
:::

## Documenting your AI use {#documenting-ai-use}

As discussed in [the previous lecture](./w8a_genAI.qmd),
journals often require you to disclose how you used genAI,
and you can't count on getting the same answer when you ask the same thing again later.
So it's a good idea to keep a record as you go. Here are two complementary ways to do so.

### Save your conversations

Claude saves your conversations automatically,
but in your Home dir rather than in your project,
and in a format that's not easy to read.
To save a conversation in your project as a plain-text file,
type `/export` in the prompt box.
In the save dialog that opens, go to (or create) an `ai-logs` dir in your project,
and give the file a descriptive name like `2026-10-14_count-reads.txt`.

Do this for conversations that helped you produce code you end up keeping,
or helped you make decisions about the analysis steps.
Consider committing these files to Git as well.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Automatically saving all conversations _(Click to expand)_

Exporting by hand is easy to forget.
To save _every_ conversation automatically, you can use a **hook**:
a shell command that Claude Code runs at a specific moment,
such as whenever Claude finishes responding.
Hooks are run by Claude Code itself rather than by the model,
so unlike instructions in `CLAUDE.md`, they always run.

A hook receives the location of Claude's own file for the current conversation,
which contains every message and tool call in a format that's hard to read.
The hook can then run a small script that converts this file
into a readable Markdown file in your project,
overwriting it each time so it stays up to date.

You don't have to write this yourself --- you can ask Claude to set it up, for example:

> Add a Stop hook to this project's `.claude/settings.json`
> that saves the current conversation as a Markdown file in `ai-logs/`.
> Name each file by the conversation's start date and session ID,
> include my prompts and your responses, and summarize each tool call in one line.

Then, have a short conversation and check the resulting Markdown file.
A few more tips:

- To use the hook in all your projects, ask Claude to put it in `~/.claude/settings.json` instead.
- Claude deletes its own conversation files from your Home dir after 30 days.
  To keep them longer, set `cleanupPeriodDays` in `~/.claude/settings.json`.
- See the [hooks documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) for details.
:::

### Let Claude keep a diary

Exported conversations are complete but long.
For a concise overview, you can let Claude keep a diary of key findings and decisions,
with an instruction in `CLAUDE.md` like this one:

```{.markdown .file filename="CLAUDE.md (excerpt)"}
## AI diary

- After completing a task, add an entry at the bottom of `doc/ai/claude-diary.md`
  with the date, what I asked for, which files you created or changed,
  and any key findings and decisions (including alternatives that were rejected)
- Keep entries short
```

Add this to your `CLAUDE.md`, start a new conversation,
and ask Claude to make a small change, for example:

> Make scripts/count_reads.sh print a usage message when no arguments are given

After editing the script, Claude should ask you for permission to create the `doc/ai`
folder (unless it already exists) and to write to `doc/ai/claude-diary.md`.

Then, open `claude-diary.md`.
Is the entry accurate, and do you think this provides enough information when you
look back at it a few months from now?

<details><summary> {{< fa lightbulb >}} Here is the entry that I got</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

```{.markdown .file filename="doc/ai/claude-diary.md"}
## 2026-10-10

- Asked: make `scripts/count_reads.sh` print a usage message when no arguments are given.
- Changed: `scripts/count_reads.sh` — added a check that prints usage to stderr
  and exits 1 when called with no args.

```

</details>

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Like any `CLAUDE.md` instruction, Claude will usually but not always follow this one.
And the diary is Claude's own summary of what happened:
read it, correct it where needed, and commit it to Git along with your code.
:::

## Managing context and cost

### Agents fill up the context window quickly

Recall from [the previous lecture](./w8a_genAI.qmd) that a model's **context window**
holds everything in the conversation, and that performance degrades as it fills up.
With an agent, this happens much faster than with a chatbot:
every file Claude reads and every command output it sees goes into the context too.

The size of the context window depends on the model.
Current Claude models can hold up to 1 million tokens (very roughly 750,000 words),
but some models and setups use a smaller window of 200,000 tokens.

To see how full the context window is, type **`/context`** in the prompt box.
At the top, this shows which model you're using,
and how many tokens are in use out of that model's context window size ---
in the example below, about 69,000 out of 200,000 tokens:

![](/img/claude-context-viz.png){fig-align="center" width="60%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the output of the /context command, showing how much of the context window is used by different categories." .lightbox}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### About the context categories _(Click to expand)_

These categories are shown in the screenshot above:

- **System prompt**: Claude Code's built-in instructions, the same in every conversation.
- **Skills**: short descriptions of available "skills"
  (see [this optional material to learn more about skills](../bonus/claude-code.qmd#skills)).
- **Messages**: everything in the conversation so far,
  including files Claude read and command output it saw.
  This grows as the conversation moves along:
  in every turn (new prompt and response), all previous messages are sent to
  the model again along with your new prompt,
  so each turn processes more tokens than the one before
  (see the box on caching below).
- **Autocompact buffer**: space reserved for summarizing the conversation once
  the context window is nearly full (see `/compact` below).
- **Free space**: what's left.

Depending on your setup, you may also see categories like:

- **Memory files**: your `CLAUDE.md` and Claude's memory notes.
- **System tools**: descriptions of the tools Claude can use, like reading files.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### Caching: what gets reprocessed with every message _(Click to expand)_

Models don't remember anything,
not even between individual rounds of prompts and answers ("turns") in a conversation.

With every new prompt, the _entire_ context
(the system prompt, your `CLAUDE.md`, and all earlier messages,
including files Claude read and command output)
is sent to the model again and processed as input tokens.

To make this faster and cheaper,
the part of the context that hasn't changed since the previous turn is **cached**:
temporarily stored, so that it doesn't need to be fully reprocessed.
Cached input tokens cost only a fraction of the regular price
(for Sonnet, about one tenth).
Only your new prompt and everything Claude does in response are processed at the full price.

However, the cache **expires** after it hasn't been used for a while,
and it's specific to a model.
After the cache expires or when you switch models,
the next message reprocesses the entire conversation at the full price.

With an API key like ours, the cache expires after only **5 minutes**
without activity.
The clock icon in the prompt box (e.g., `4m`) shows how much time is left.
(With a personal subscription, Claude Code keeps the cache for an hour instead:
that costs more per cached token, which doesn't matter with a fixed monthly fee
but does when you pay per token.)

Some practical consequences:

- When you come back to a long conversation after a break
  of more than a few minutes,
  consider starting a new conversation instead,
  unless you really need what was discussed before.
- Choose your model at the start of a conversation,
  rather than switching back and forth during it.
- Even with caching, every turn in a long conversation costs more,
  sometimes significantly more, than one in a short conversation,
  which is another reason to [start fresh often](#start-fresh).
:::

### Start fresh often {#start-fresh}

Throughout this session, we've started a **new conversation** for each new task.
That's a good habit:
Claude can get confused when you switch topics within a conversation,
and a long conversation is slower and more expensive.

In a new conversation, Claude is at least in principle completely **unaware** of
what was said in earlier ones.
However, it does read your `CLAUDE.md` and its own memory notes,
and it may read files like a diary (as discussed above),
either on its own or because `CLAUDE.md` tells it to.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### The `/clear` and `/compact` slash commands _(Click to expand)_

Two slash commands related to this:

- **`/clear`** (or `/new`) also starts a new conversation.
  It may look like it deletes the current conversation,
  because it doesn't visibly switch to a new one like the `+` icon does,
  but the previous conversation is still available under the clock icon.

- **`/compact`** replaces the conversation so far with a summary, to free up space.
  Claude also does this automatically when the context window is nearly full.
  This is useful and clever behavior, though details can get lost in the process.
:::

### Cost

Every token costs money, and your API key has a limited budget:
an initial $10, which we may increase later in the semester if needed.
That may sound like a lot, but even a basic question often costs tens of cents,
and a longer agentic task considerably more.
We already pointed out that bigger models cost more per token,
and that higher effort levels use more tokens per task.
Some other things to know:

- **Output tokens** (Claude's responses, including its "thinking")
  cost several times more than input tokens.

- **Agentic tasks** can use many tokens, even when the visible conversation is short,
  because Claude reads files and command outputs behind the scenes.

- **Large data files**:
  if Claude reads an entire FASTQ or BAM file, that alone can use up much of your budget.
  It's smart about using commands like `head` and `grep` to avoid doing this,
  but make sure you don't ask it explicitly to "read" large data files^[
    As pointed out before: Claude should help you write code that reads and analyzes
    data, rather than reading and "analyzing" data itself.].

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

To see an **estimate** of what the current conversation has cost so far,
type `/usage` --- example output is shown in the screenshot on the right.

This information is somewhat limited, e.g. you can't see usage for other conversations,
or how much you've used in total for this API key.

(When you have a personal subscription, more detailed usage information is provided.)

:::
::: {.column width="55%"}

![](/img/claude-usage-api-screenshot.png){fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the output of the /usage command, showing how many input and output tokens have been used, and an estimated cost." .lightbox}

:::
:::

::: callout-tip
#### You don't always need an agent
For general questions, like explaining a concept or a command,
a browser-based chat like Gemini (through your OSU account) works just as well
and doesn't use your API key's budget.
Use Claude when it helps that it can see your files and run commands.

If you _do_ ask Claude Code simpler questions that don't require it to read files
or run commands, it sometimes helps to explicitly tell it to
*"answer based on first principles"* or *"don't read any files"*.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### API pricing vs. personal subscriptions _(Click to expand)_
Paying per token through an API key, as we do here, is **much** more expensive than
a personal subscription to a service like Claude, which has a fixed monthly fee.
A day of heavy agentic coding through an API can easily cost more than a month's subscription.

If you want to try Claude for personal projects
(and/or projects that don't involve institutional data),
a personal subscription is worth considering for this reason ---
though it will then be _you_ who's paying.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Using a personal account in a research project _(Click to expand)_

Personal accounts are not approved for institutional data,
which includes your unpublished research data.
But much of what an AI agent helps you with only involves your **code**.
So you _may_ be able to use a personal account in a research project,
as long as you make sure that the AI can't see your data:

- **Make Claude ignore files** with a deny rule
  (see [permission rules](../bonus/claude-code.qmd#permission-rules)),
  such as `"Read(//fs/ess/PAS1234/myproject/data/**)"`.
  This blocks Claude's own file reads as well as common commands like `cat` and `head`,
  but not, for example, a script that opens the files by itself.

- **Keep your data outside the workspace.**
  Claude reads files in your workspace without asking,
  but asks for permission before accessing anything outside of it.
  This is at odds with our recommendation to keep everything for a project
  in one [self-contained project dir](../week02/w2a_project-org.qmd),
  which you then open as your workspace.
  But you can keep that project structure and open only a subdir as the workspace:
  for example, open `myproject/scripts` rather than `myproject`,
  and decline any request to access `myproject/data`.
  The downside is that Claude can then also not freely see the rest of your project,
  such as your results and README.

Keep in mind that anything that ends up in the conversation is sent to the AI,
including the output of commands it runs (e.g. a script that prints part of your data)
and anything you paste into a prompt.
And none of the above is watertight.
When in doubt, check with your advisor, or use an OSU-approved tool.

:::

## Good habits when working with an agent

#### Getting good help

- **Be explicit.** Point Claude to the relevant files, and put your conventions and rules
  in `CLAUDE.md`.
- **Start fresh** for each new task, and keep conversations focused.
- **Use it to raise your standards.** Ask it for things that make code more robust
  but are easy to skip, like input checks, usage messages, comments, and a README [@king2026].

#### Checking and keeping the results

- **You own the result.** Read every proposed edit and command before approving it.
- **Verify, don't trust.** When Claude says something "works", that may be a prediction
  rather than a test result. Run the code yourself, and check results independently.
- **Results should come from code you can rerun.** Let Claude help you write code that you
  review, run, and keep; don't rely on numbers or conclusions it only reports in the chat.
- **Commit before, review after.** Use Git so that you can see and undo what Claude changed.
- **Keep a record.** Commit the code that Claude helped write,
  and [document how you used AI](#documenting-ai-use), for example with exported conversations
  and a diary. You can't count on getting the same answer if you ask again later.

#### Protecting secrets and data

- **Keep secrets out of prompts.** Never paste passwords or API keys into a prompt.
- **Remember that Claude can see what you can see.** In shared dirs like `/fs/ess/PAS3493`,
  that may include other people's files and data. Keep Claude's workspace limited to your own project.

## Ideas for using agentic AI

So far, we've used Claude for fairly small tasks.
Here are some ideas for what else it can be useful for in your research:

- **Troubleshooting complex errors**\
  Agents can be very good at following the trail of an error through a complicated
  set of scripts or a workflow.
- **Things that are beyond your ability, but easy to verify**\
  For example, a complicated software installation,
  or automating a tedious, repetitive task.
- **Proofreading code that works**\
  In a large set of scripts, it's easy to miss inconsistent variable names or similar
  small errors --- agents can be quite meticulous at catching these.
